title: Code Quality Check
description: Predict which patterns count as code smells and why they matter for maintainability.

questions.prompt: A function works correctly on the happy path but still has a leftover `console.log("debugging", items)` call. Is this a code smell worth flagging?

options.text: No — if the logic is correct, nothing else matters
Yes — debug output left in shipped code pollutes logs and signals the code wasn't cleaned up
No — console.log is always required for production debugging
Only if the function also throws an error

questions.explanation: Code smells are about maintainability risk, not just correctness on the happy path. Leftover debug logging is a classic sign of incomplete cleanup.

questions.prompt: Why is `var` considered a smell in modern JavaScript, even in code that currently works?

options.text: `var` is slower than `let`/`const` at runtime
`var` is function-scoped and hoisted, which can leak variables and enable rebinding bugs that `let`/`const` prevent
`var` was removed from the language and no longer works
`var` cannot hold numbers

questions.explanation: `var`'s function scoping and hoisting create surprises that `let`/`const` avoid via block scoping and the temporal dead zone.

questions.prompt: What does a `// TODO: handle empty array` comment signal to a code reviewer?

options.text: The author already handled every edge case perfectly
The author is aware of a known gap that was left unresolved before this code was submitted
TODOs are purely decorative and carry no information
The function will throw an error immediately

questions.explanation: A TODO comment documents a known, acknowledged gap — useful for tracking, but a smell if it's left in code being reviewed as "done."

questions.prompt: When flagging a code smell in review, what should accompany the flag?

options.text: Nothing — just say "this is bad" and move on
A one-sentence reason for what could go wrong later, not just a style preference
A demand to rewrite the entire file from scratch
A link to an unrelated style guide with no explanation

questions.explanation: Naming the concrete risk (e.g., "empty array silently returns 0, which might be wrong") is more persuasive and educational than a bare style objection.

questions.prompt: A snippet has correct logic but includes `var`, a leftover `console.log`, and an unresolved `TODO`. How many maintainability smells does this contain?

options.text: Zero — correct logic means no smells
One — only the most severe issue counts
Three — `var`, `console.log`, and `TODO` are each independent smells
It's impossible to have more than one smell in the same function

questions.explanation: Each pattern is an independent maintainability risk; a snippet can have multiple smells simultaneously even if it runs correctly.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between a "bug" and a "code smell"?

options.text: A bug means the code produces a wrong result now; a smell is a maintainability risk that may not affect correctness today
They mean exactly the same thing
A smell always means the tests will fail
A bug is always caused by a code smell

questions.explanation: Code smells (leftover logs, TODOs, var) don't necessarily break the happy path — that's exactly why they're easy to miss and worth flagging anyway.
